newsitem.title: USA: FCC review of NYNEX seen by some as Justice rebuke.
newsitem.headline: FCC review of NYNEX seen by some as Justice rebuke.

text.p: The Federal Communications Commission is carefully scrutinizing the proposed merger of Bell Atlantic Corp and NYNEX Corp in what critics read as a rebuke of the Justice Department's decision to give the deal unconditional approval.
But government officials say their departments are doing the jobs they are supposed to do, without stepping on each other's turf.
And no one -- even the critics -- expects the FCC review to derail the $23 billion merger of the two giant East Coast telephone companies, although it is causing some delay.

"Effectively, the FCC is trying to mop up for the Justice Department mistakes that are endangering competition and threatening higher prices for telephone service," said Gene Kimmelman of Consumers' Union. "Unfortunately, it may be too little too late."
An industry source familiar with the FCC negotiations said the talks delaying the merger will not last forever.
"We expect that they will conclude in July," he said. "They are focused on steps that could be taken to further open the market in New York."
If that happened, the FCC would do what the Justice Department did not -- impose conditions on the merger.

Under the law, phone companies must make their systems available to potential competitors. The FCC is asking the companies to change their billing equipment, making it easier and cheaper for competitors to use, a source familiar with the talks said. The phone companies are ready to do that within the next 18 months.

Should the Justice Department have imposed that requirement first, as critics say? Those at antitrust agencies have always viewed their responsibilities as different from those of regulatory agencies like the FCC.
The Justice Department is a law enforcement agency, which looks at deals narrowly to determine if they are anticompetitive and violate the law.
The FCC is a regulatory agency, which oversees broadcast stations and telephone companiess. Before it passes on proposals, it has a broad mandate to determine if they are in the public interest.
Historically, antitrust enforcement agencies have been reluctant to step into regulation. And the FCC's proposals, defenders of the agencies say, are more regulatory than enforcement.

The FCC review "is not a critique (of Justice) or a statement or anything like that," an FCC official emphasized. "The FCC's review is the FCC's independent duty and it's not about anything except whether this merger would serve the public interest."
But such fine distinctions cut no ice with critics.
For example, Sen. Ernest Hollings, a South Carolina Democrat, has placed a "hold" on the confirmation of Joel Klein to head the Justice Department's antitrust division.
It was Klein who, as acting chief of the antitrust division, decided against taking the merger to court.
"He feels Mr. Klein continually misreads the telecommunications act," a spokesman said. "This merger is one of the prime examples which makes Mr. Klein's nomination unacceptable."
